items.gist: The ever-arisen supreme heart is one's own self-reflection, and spanda is the stirring of the self.
Even slight movement is a wave of the ocean of awareness; the inert world depends on consciousness as its essence.
Without the rise of will, knowledge, and action there is no being; visarga is projected and reabsorbed by supreme awareness.
After reabsorption, the three powers are internalized, and the uncreated parāmarśa is the shining of 'I'.
This power is the heart of all mantras; any action performed from the heart counts as japa, and spontaneous creation is true meditation.
For seekers, a limited form is meditated upon, but the fully hearted yogin has no desire for fruit.
The yogin's bodily state is a mudrā, and beings entering the fire of awareness become homa.
The purified initiate stands firm; through varied manifestations of consciousness, duality is abandoned and one becomes Bhairava.
As one sees one's face in a mirror, seeing oneself as Bhairava in ritual leads to becoming one with him, the supreme fullness.
This yāga exists in the heart of some; one who matures in it attains kaivalya while still embodied.
In this yāga there is no purity or impurity, no liṅga worship, no renunciation, and no prescribed or forbidden act.
The yogin must steady the mind in truth; one established in truth is untouched by impurity, like a lotus leaf by water.
Purity and impurity cannot be established by mutual dependence; mantras are naturally pure because of Śiva-nature.
Purity for the yogin is in being; scriptural injunctions are not simply invalidated but applied with proper scope.
The Śaiva scripture is not false; arthavāda is authoritative in its own domain of freedom.
The injunction is not meaningless; impurity proclaimed for a dead body does not apply elsewhere, since consciousness has fallen away.
